steps.body: Most divisions leave something over. The remainder is what could not form another whole group — and it is always smaller than the divisor.
steps.narration: Most divisions leave something over. The remainder is what could not form another whole group — and it is always smaller than the divisor.

widget.prompt: 47 hikers into groups of 6. Hop by sixes and see how far you get.

commonLandings.feedback: Eight hops overshoot 47; only seven full groups of six fit inside it.
Six hops leave eleven over, which is more than six — another whole group still fits.

widget.missFeedback: Each hop is 6. From 0, 7 hops land on 42.
widget.successFeedback: 42 after seven hops — five hikers short of 47, and those five are the remainder.

predict.prompt: Dividing 47 by 6, can the remainder be 8?
predict.reveal: A remainder of 8 still contains a whole group of 6, so the quotient was counted one too low.

cml.actionGoal: Split a factor into places, build each piece, and reassemble the whole for g4m remainder.
invariants: Splitting a factor never changes the product: every piece of the split multiplies the other factor, and the pieces add back to exactly the same total, which is what makes g4m remainder decomposable at all.
misconceptions: Adding only some of the partial products, dropping or inventing a zero when factors carry tens, or letting a remainder reach or exceed the divisor.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If one partial product were left out, exactly how much of the total would go missing?

widget.prompt: Divide 23 by 3. The quotient is 7. What is the remainder?

commonErrors.feedback: A remainder can never reach the divisor — 3 more would make one more whole group.
7 is how many full groups formed; the remainder is what is left over after them.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Split a factor into its places, multiply each part, and add every piece back.

steps.body: If the remainder reached the divisor, one more group could be made. That is the test: a remainder at or above the divisor means the quotient is too small.
